Guard hair.deeper: In double-coated goats, primary follicles grow coarse guard hair and secondary follicles grow the fine down sold as cashmere. The two populations barely overlap: in one study of Changthangi goats guard hair averaged about 68 microns in diameter against about 13 microns for down, and guard hair in Bakerwal and Kargil goats exceeded 100 microns. Proteomic comparison of cashmere, guard hair and sheep wool detected 159, 204 and 70 proteins respectively and pointed to the keratin KRT85 and the keratin-associated proteins KRTAP15-1 and KRTAP3-1 as candidate markers of diameter differences. Within a herd, guard-hair length correlates positively with guard-hair diameter and with down length. Guard hairs are often medullated, and an air-filled core raises light reflection and gives a chalky appearance, one reason residual coarse fibers are measured rather than judged by eye.
Guard hair.origins: The distinction matters commercially wherever the underfur, not the outer coat, is the product. Beyond cashmere, researchers applied wool and cashmere test methods to qiviut, the down of the muskox, sampling 299 wild animals harvested on Banks Island, Canada, in 1997. They reported a theoretical yield defined as the percentage by mass of fibers of 30 microns or less, the same threshold US law uses to limit coarse fibers in cashmere.

Hand.deeper: Instrumental hand assessment treats touch as a response to small deformations. The Kawabata Evaluation System for Fabrics (KES-F) applies small forces and strains with four instruments: KES-FB1 for tensile and shear, KES-FB2 for bending, KES-FB3 for compression and KES-FB4 for surface friction and geometric roughness. Together they yield a panel of characteristic values (one common tabulation counts eighteen), such as bending rigidity, shear hysteresis, compressional resilience and coefficient of friction. Regression equations derived from expert panel judgments convert those values into primary hand values, including koshi (stiffness), numeri (smoothness), fukurami (fullness and softness), shari (crispness) and hari (anti-drape stiffness), and then into a total hand value on a 0 to 5 scale for a specified end use. Because the equations are built for particular end uses, a hand value calculated for one fabric category should not be read as a universal softness score.
Hand.origins: Attempts to measure hand began with Peirce, whose 1930 paper 'The handle of cloth as a measurable quantity' (Journal of the Textile Institute Transactions, volume 21) introduced a cantilever bending test. In 1972 Sueo Kawabata, then a professor at Kyoto University, founded the Hand Evaluation and Standardization Committee, made up of experienced specialists from the Japanese textile industry. The committee agreed on Japanese descriptive terms for primary hand qualities and selected graded standard fabrics, and Kawabata's instrument system, designed from the same year, aimed to predict those expert judgments from measurement.

Knitting.deeper: A knit is described by courses, the rows of loops across the fabric, and wales, the columns along it. In weft knitting one yarn feeds across successive needles to form a course; in warp knitting each needle receives its own yarn, and loops interconnect along the length, which usually makes the fabric more stable and less prone to laddering. Loop length governs relaxed dimensions, and tightness factor is commonly the square root of yarn tex divided by loop length. Residual yarn torque can rotate loops and cause spirality in single jersey. Comparative studies with fixed machine settings find that both fiber type and knit structure affect bursting strength, pilling, abrasion and wicking. Open loops also shed more: in one laundering study, untreated polyester knit released about 24 fibers per square centimeter against about 17 for a woven, which the authors attributed to the woven's more compact structure.
Knitting.origins: Mechanized weft knitting made single jersey a staple of underwear and T-shirt production on circular machines, which produce it as a tube at high speed, and hand knitters know the same structure as stockinette. Knits now dominate everyday garments: in a 2026 study of 9,333 items donated to Canadian thrift stores, 64.7 percent were knitted structures, a mix that shapes what post-consumer sorting and recycling must handle.

Micron.deeper: Wool diameter is measured by methods recognized by the International Wool Textile Organisation (IWTO), which lists five. The projection microscope (IWTO-8) is the reference: fiber snippets are projected at 500 times magnification and measured one by one, which also allows the percentage of medullated fibers to be counted. Airflow methods (IWTO-28 for raw-wool core samples, IWTO-6 for combed sliver) infer a mean indirectly from how a compressed plug of fibers resists the passage of air, and are calibrated against the projection microscope. The Sirolan-Laserscan (IWTO-12, also ASTM D6466) and the Optical Fibre Diameter Analyser, OFDA (IWTO-47), measure large numbers of individual snippets optically and report the distribution as well as the mean. Because the methods sample and weight fibers differently, airflow and image-based results for the same lot can show systematic differences, so lots should be compared on the same method.
Micron.origins: The projection microscope, using instruments such as the WIRA microscope and the Lanameter calibrated with a graticule, became the reference method against which faster techniques were calibrated. The airflow instrument was extended to raw wool when IWTO accepted test method IWTO-28 in 1971, allowing mean diameter of sale lots to be certified from core samples. In 1995 IWTO accepted both the Laserscan (IWTO-12) and OFDA (IWTO-47) methods for raw wool and top certification, which made routine reporting of diameter variability practical alongside the mean micron figure.
